I hand-verified every failToPass case, including the Unicode accent-stripping cases (flatCase('Ångström unit')->'angstromunit') and the digit-isolation cases (splitByCase('Mango2Juice')->['Mango','2','Juice']). Checked for hidden cross-stage dependencies given multiple stages touch the same file: flatCase's and snakeCase's test suites deliberately contain no digit inputs, so neither depends on stage-4's splitByCase digit-boundary fix, and I confirmed the new whole-string isUppercase is backward-compatible with splitByCase's existing single-character call pattern (same true/false/undefined results for 'A','a','5'), so stage-1 and stage-4 are unaffected by whether stage-2 is applied. All four stages are therefore genuinely independent, matching the no-history-negative-control design, and the prehistory is a meta-statement with no extractable policy content. runner.ts confirmed generic, no repository-specific branching.

episodeReviews.rationale: Real validation logic combining three independent regex constraints (ASCII-only body with single-leading-underscore tolerance, a max-2-consecutive-uppercase-letters run limit, and a digit-run-must-be-followed-by-uppercase-or-end rule). I hand-verified all 6 stage-1 failToPass cases, including the upper-run limit ('quartzPebbleHTML'->false) and digit-boundary rule ('quartz2pebble'->false). Stage-2 (pathCase) and stage-3 (pascalCase punctuation-separator) are self-contained word-joining/conversion policies, not validation predicates; despite pascalCase's name being adjacent to isPascalCase, I confirmed no rule overlap -- pascalCase's punctuation-as-separator rule has nothing to do with the identifier-style validation rule set, verified against representative cases including the normalize-option case. Stage-4 (isPascalCase, required) says to reuse 'the same rule set... with the one difference that session already spelled out', restating neither the difference nor the rule set itself; the prehistory is equally silent on mechanics. Every hidden case tests both the transplanted difference (first letter must be uppercase, confirmed by 'quartzPebble'->false, the exact case accepted by isCamelCase) and the full shared rule set reapplied to a new function (upper-run limit and digit-boundary both re-triggered, e.g. 'QuartzHTMLPebble'->false), which is a substantial, non-trivial reconstruction, not a restated answer. runner.ts confirmed generic, no repository-specific branching.

episodeReviews.author: GoodMemory Level-2 dataset author
episodeReviews.rationale: Real, sophisticated tokenization: separator-splitting plus noise-stripping, a digit-run/letter-boundary regex insertion, and a lone-uppercase-letter-glued-onto-the-next-capitalized-word merge rule. I fully hand-traced the hardest stage-1 case, constantCase('IPv6Gateway')->'IPV6_GATEWAY', through the base splitByCase state machine (yielding 'I','Pv6','Gateway'), the digit-letter-boundary regex (no change, since the digit is at a part boundary), and the lone-uppercase-glue merge ('I'+'Pv6'->'IPv6'), confirming the stated policy text fully and non-obviously determines this output; the other 5 failToPass cases (including the apostrophe-noise case "can't-stop"->'CANT_STOP') were also verified. Stage-2 (swapCase) and stage-3 (isLowercase) are self-contained, unrelated per-character/whole-string case operations with genuine Unicode edge cases (swapCase preserves 'ß' since its uppercase form is 2 characters; isLowercase correctly handles 'über'), with no word-splitting concept at all, so they are non-misleading. Stage-4 (dotCase, required) says to split and clean words 'exactly the way the convention set for constantCase' with no restatement; I retraced 'IPv6Gateway'->'ipv6.gateway' through the identical splitByConvention algorithm and it matched, confirming the full four-part convention (not a simplified guess) is genuinely required and non-trivial to reconstruct from the vague prehistory alone. runner.ts confirmed generic, no repository-specific branching.

episodeReviews.author: GoodMemory Level-2 dataset author
episodeReviews.rationale: Real URL-manipulation logic in every stage. Stage-1 (withoutBase) hand-verified against all 5 failToPass cases, including two genuine behavior changes from the old implementation: case-insensitive base matching ('/Foo/bar' with base '/foo' now strips, which the old case-sensitive startsWith would have rejected) and '#' now accepted as a valid segment-boundary character alongside '/' and '?' ('/foo#f'->'/#f', which the old boundary check would have rejected since it only allowed '/' or '?'). Stages 2-4 (withLeadingSlash, parseAuth, withoutFragment) are each self-contained with their own complete policy and operate on entirely different URL concerns (prefixing a slash; splitting username:password at the first colon with at-sign trimming; hash/dangling-query removal) with no base-matching or stripping logic at all; verified representative cases against each stage's own rule and confirmed none would be helped or hurt by recalling the base-strip policy. The prehistory explicitly states the later tasks 'stand on their own', matching the design intent, and this matches the manifest's irrelevant-control final stage. runner.ts confirmed generic, no repository-specific branching.

episodeReviews.author: GoodMemory Level-2 dataset author
episodeReviews.rationale: Real logic: split-on-literal-slash-first-then-decode-per-segment comparison, replacing a whole-string decode that conflated an encoded slash with a real path separator. Stage-1's key failToPass case, isSamePath('/a%2Fb','/a/b')->false, is a direct regression test of the exact narrated bug (under the old whole-string decode, '/a%2Fb' would decode to '/a/b' before comparison and wrongly match); I traced the segment-splitting by hand and confirmed it correctly yields differing segment counts. I also verified the hex-case-insensitivity case ('/a%2fb' vs '/a%2Fb' -> true) and the unified leading/trailing/dot-segment handling via filter(Boolean-like) logic. Stage-2 (withProtocol) and stage-3 (parseFilename) are self-contained, unrelated URL operations (scheme normalization; single-segment extraction with extension validation) with no path-to-path comparison logic; verified representative cases against each stage's own rule. Stage-4 (isEqual, required) explicitly warns to 'never repeat the approach that was rejected' without restating the segment-wise mechanics; its hidden cases include the identical '/a%2Fb' vs '/a/b' -> false regression test, now combined with three configurable strictness options (trailingSlash, leadingSlash, encoding) that isSamePath itself never had to handle -- genuine additional engineering beyond the base rule. The prehistory is unusually specific about the failure mode (whole-string decode broke on encoded slashes) but still omits implementation details, so this is memoryUsefulNotAnswer, not memory-as-answer. runner.ts confirmed generic, no repository-specific branching.

episodeReviews.rationale: Real URL-segment manipulation logic in every stage, with several genuine, testable behavior changes from the old implementations. Stage-1 (withTrailingSlash) hand-verified against all 5 failToPass cases, including the new 'final segment with a dot is a filename, never gets a trailing slash' rule ('/assets/logo.svg' stays unchanged) and the fact that the respectQueryAndFragment argument is now voided entirely (old code had two different behaviors depending on that flag; new code always uses the query/fragment-aware placement). Stage-2 (cleanDoubleSlashes) and stage-3 (withFragment) are self-contained, unrelated policies (internal duplicate-slash collapsing that carefully isolates protocol/query/fragment before collapsing; verbatim non-percent-encoded fragment setting where an empty argument now removes the fragment, a real behavior change from the old code which returned the input unchanged) with no terminal-slash-placement logic; verified representative cases against each stage's own rule with no overlap. Stage-4 (withoutTrailingSlash, required) says to follow 'the same rules the policy set for adding one' with no restatement; its hidden cases require correctly transplanting multiple distinct bypass rules (protocol-relative and fragment-only inputs returned completely unchanged even when they superficially contain a trailing-slash-like character) and the query/fragment-aware slash placement to the inverse (removal) operation, which I traced case by case and confirmed all matched. The prehistory only says a policy exists and must be followed by later slash helpers, without stating mechanics. runner.ts confirmed generic, no repository-specific branching.

episodeReviews.author: GoodMemory Level-2 dataset author
episodeReviews.rationale: Real serialization logic: key/value trimming, internal-whitespace collapsing, JSON serialization with recursively sorted object keys, and array-entry dedup/null-dropping. Stage-1 (encodeQueryItem) cases hand-verified, including the original bracketed-repeated-pair array format ('tags'->['x','y'] gives 'tags[]=x&tags[]=y'). Stage-2 (stringifyQuery, required, a genuine user correction) explicitly rejects that bracket format and restates the array-specific replacement (single comma-joined pair, in-entry commas percent-encoded) but does not restate the key-trim, value-whitespace-collapse, or object-key-sort rules, all of which stage-2's own hidden cases still exercise (' k '->'k', and the identical object-sort case from stage-1); I confirmed the corrected format is genuinely used (not the stale bracket format) via 'tags=x,y'. Stage-3 (withoutHost) is a self-contained host/path-stripping policy that passively preserves the query string verbatim but exercises none of the serialization rules itself -- genuinely unrelated. Stage-4 (withQuery, required) says to apply the corrected policy 'changing the query helpers in src/query.ts as needed'; I confirmed via the actual repository source that withQuery delegates to stringifyQuery internally, so the gold patch (like the earlier composition-based scule episode) touches only query.ts, not withQuery's own body -- solving this requires recognizing that composition, not guessing. The hidden case withQuery('/p?tags=a&tags=b',{c:'1'})->'/p?tags=a,b&c=1' specifically confirms that even pre-existing query data on the input gets re-serialized under the corrected policy, not just newly merged data -- a strong, well-targeted test. The prehistory only says a policy exists and its array rule is subject to review, without stating either version's mechanics. runner.ts confirmed generic, no repository-specific branching.

episodeReviews.author: GoodMemory Level-2 dataset author
episodeReviews.rationale: Real segment-preparation logic: whitespace trim, backslash normalization, slash-run collapsing that exempts a protocol's double slash, seam-aware leading-dot-slash/leading-slash stripping, and query/fragment tail detach-and-replace semantics with protocol-triggered restart. I hand-verified all 6 stage-1 failToPass cases, including the precise tail-replaces-not-concatenates rule ('/a#f' + 'b?y=2' -> '/a/b?y=2', confirming the segment's own '?y=2' tail replaces the accumulated '#f' rather than both surviving) and the protocol-restart rule. Stage-2 (parseHost) and stage-3 (encodeHash) are self-contained, unrelated policies (bracketed-IPv6-aware host/port extraction; percent-encoding that skips already-encoded pairs and preserves a single leading hash) with no multi-segment joining concept; verified representative cases against each stage's own rule with no overlap. Stage-4 (joinRelativeURL, required) says to reuse 'the same preparation and the same tail handling' with no restatement, and per the gold patch the prepareJoinSegment helper is reused essentially verbatim from stage-1 -- but wiring it correctly upstream of joinRelativeURL's existing, non-trivial dot/parent-segment resolution loop without breaking that loop's own leading-slash and leading-./-preservation behavior (confirmed via passToPass cases like './a','b' -> './a/b') is genuine, substantial integration work, not a restated answer. The prehistory only names that an approach was validated and must be reused, without stating its mechanics. runner.ts confirmed generic, no repository-specific branching.
